layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract—Three austenitic stainless steels (a Fe-17Cr-13Ni-0.15N alloy, an ultra pure Fe-18Cr-10Ni

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloy and a type 304 stainless steel) were used in this study in order to investigate the effect of nitrogen on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the electrochemical behaviour and on the nature of the passive film formed on the steels in acidic solution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: . The presence of nitrogen in the alloy does not apparently have a significant influence on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the response of the material to anodic polarization in the acid electrolyte. Surface analysis of the alloys by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: XPS after passivation shows that nitrogen is enriched at the surface by anodic segregation during

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolution and passivation of the nitrogen-bearing alloys. After passivation of the alloys three chemical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: states of nitrogen are detected in the N 1s spectrum. The peak at low binding energy (397.7 ± 0.1 eV)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to nitrogen bonded essentially to chromium under the form of a nitride which is incorporated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the passive film. The N 1s peaks observed at higher binding energies (400.2 ± 0.1 and 402 ± 0.1 cV)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correspond to nitrogen species located on the surface of the passivated alloys, which are produced by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reaction of the alloy surface with the solution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In the presence of both nitrogen and molybdenum, significant improvements in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resistance of stainless steels to general and localized corrosion have been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reported.1-5 However, it remains unclear if nitrogen alone (i.e. in the absence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum) is capable of improving the corrosion resistance. It has been shown in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a recent study that nitrogen implanted into a type 304 stainless steel does not improve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the dissolution and passivation behaviour in acid solution.º Nitrogen can be added to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steels in order to stabilize the austenite phase and thus it is important to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elucidate the role of this element in the passivity of the alloy. The aim of this work

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was to investigate, by electrochemical and surface analytical measurements, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effect of nitrogen on the dissolution and passivation of austenitic stainless steel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: without molybdenum. In order to clearly identify the effect of nitrogen, two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: synthetic alloys were studied, one without and the other with nitrogen. A type 304

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steel was also studied for comparison.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: In order to investigate the effect of time of polarization and potential on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1050 mV(SHE), for 1, 15, 30 and 120 min. The N 1s XPS spectrum recorded after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 30 min at 650 mV(SHE) and at 1050 mV(SHE) are shown in Fig. 5c. The recorded

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decreases with the time of polarization for the first ~15-30 min and then becomes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constant. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: signal first increases and becomes constant after ~15-30 min of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: the growth of the passive film covering the nitride causes the attenuation of the signal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emitted by N(1) at the interface. The N(1) signal becomes constant when the passive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: film has reached a stationary thickness.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CONCLUSIONS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The electrochemical behaviour and the surface composition of Fe-17Cr-13Ni–

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 0.15N stainless steel have been investigated with special emphasis on the role of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nitrogen. The addition of nitrogen does not improve the general corrosion behaviour

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the alloy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: After passivation of the alloy, three chemical states of nitrogen are detected: the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high and intermediate binding energy peaks are assigned to nitrogen species located

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the surface of the passive film and are produced at least in part via reaction with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electrolyte. The peak at low binding energy corresponds to N-metal (essentially Cr)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bonds under the form of nitride, present in the inner part of the passive film near the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passive film/alloy interface. This nitride phase is formed by anodic segregation of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nitrogen contained in the alloy, during the dissolution stage preceding passivation.
